In the second piece, the author checks up on Jeremy Brown, one of the controversial amateur baseball players selected by the A's in the 2002 draft. Brown is mocked for his weight, but his talent is visible in the training sessions he attends. At the end, Brown scores a home run in a practice game but falls over while running around the bases, not realizing he has hit the ball out of the park.
In the afterword the author responds to various criticisms of the book. Most come from baseball insiders and journalists, acidly referred to by Lewis as "The Club." Insiders condemn his book, but in fact, few of these critics have read it. Some attribute its authorship to Beane, asserting Beane secretly wrote it, which is not the truth.

Conventional wisdom long held that big name, highly athletic hitters and young pitchers with rocket arms were the ticket to success. But Beane and his staff, buoyed by massive amounts of carefully interpreted statistical data, believed that wins could be had by more affordable methods such as hitters with high on-base percentage and pitchers who get lots of ground outs. ## About This Book

What happens when an underfunded baseball team decides to stop trusting its own eyes? In Moneyball, Michael Lewis follows Billy Beane, the Oakland A's general manager who concluded that baseball's oldest instincts were mostly wrong — and then bet his career on it. Armed with overlooked statistics and players no one else wanted, Beane set out to compete against franchises spending three times his budget. The stakes are both concrete and philosophical: a single season's wins and losses, yes, but also the larger question of whether data can outthink decades of human intuition in any field.

Lewis has a rare gift for turning institutional conflict into page-turning narrative, and Moneyball is where that gift runs at full speed.
